newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian government warns foreign press.
newsitem.headline: Serbian government warns foreign press.

text.p: The government warned foreign journalists over their reporting of Serbia's political crisis on Sunday as opposition parties girded for a battle with the authorities over press freedom.

The Zajedno (Together) coalition, whose street protests forced the government to recognise its election victories in Serbia's main towns, has threatened to resume demonstrations unless media controls are relaxed by March 9.
Zajedno leaders believe access to the state media will be crucial to their chances of beating the ruling Socialist Party (SPS) in parliamentary and presidential elections later this year.

The warning to foreign journalists by Information Minister Radmila Milentijevic signalled that the government would not give ground without a fight and would try to spread its influence over information to the foreign media.

She told the pro-government daily Politika: "We must especially hold (foreign journalists) responsible for what they write. This means that if they write something which is not factually correct, we should react and demand that the untruth be corrected."

Milentijevic, a newly appointed loyalist to President Slobodan Milosevic, added: "In view of the force and influence the media exert on the shaping of public opinion and government policy, their responsibility is exceptional."

In its last crackdown on the foreign media in 1994, at the height of the war in Bosnia, Serbia refused to renew the accreditations of almost 20 foreign journalists whose reporting the authorities disliked.

Although Serbia has no censorship, the main broadcast and print media are under strict state control. Independent radios have limited range and the government rations the supply of newsprint to independent newspapers and magazines.
The limited reporting by state television on three months of Zajedno and student demonstrations against SPS attempts to rig the local election results was hostile to the opposition.
The opposition called off the demonstrations on Saturday but set a new deadline for Milosevic in its campaign to end half a century of Socialist rule in Serbia.

Zajedno leadr Zoran Djindjic told supporters: "Let us give them a chance to show an intention to free the media and, if they fail to do that by March 9, then what else can we do but go out into the streets again."

Another of the three opposition leaders, Vuk Draskovic, described that victory over the local election results as "only the first step, but an enormous step. "We cannot change the passengers in our bus, but we must change the driver."
The opposition will hold a celebration party on Friday to mark the first session of the opposition-led local council in Belgrade.
"Prepare well, because it will be jolly and it could last all night," said opposition co-leader Vesna Pesic.

Belgrade students who have also held daily protests said they would continue their demonstrations until the government sacked the university rector and prosecuted those responsible for annulling the local election results.
